_comment: Hand-authored content for the public site. Everything else on the site is
generated from docs/**/*.md, so this file holds only the things that have
no markdown source: the landing page's video slots, the SEO metadata, and
the FAQ block that search engines read as structured data.
The build fails loudly on anything here that points at a file which does
not exist. That is deliberate — a silently-broken poster or a stale slug
is worse than a build error, because it ships.
MAIN WALKTHROUGH — the one video on the landing page.
`id` is a YouTube video id and is EMPTY until one is recorded. While it
is empty the section renders nothing at all; it does not render a broken
player. So this block is safe to leave as-is indefinitely.
TO ADD ONE:
1. Upload to YouTube (unlisted is fine — it still embeds and still
gets indexed as VideoObject structured data).
2. Put the id here, plus uploadDate (YYYY-MM-DD) and duration in ISO 8601
(PT4M13S = 4m13s). Both feed the structured data; wrong values are
worse than absent ones.
3. Fill in each chapter's `start`. The chapter list becomes jump links
under the player and SEO clip markers.
4. `poster` is a repo-relative image path. Leave empty to use YouTube's
own thumbnail.

_comment: GUIDE VIDEOS — one short upload per how-to page, keyed by the page slug
exactly as it appears in the site generator's root-page list.
Why per-page rather than one long walkthrough: a video costs a re-record
every time the thing it shows changes, so the split that pays is along
change-rate boundaries. A guide covering somebody else's interface — the
Discord Developer Portal, Foundry's module installer — never churns when
this project releases. A guide covering this app's own dashboard churns
with every interface change, so keep those steps TOGETHER in one video.
That lands at a handful of videos, not one per page.

howTo.name: Install Tusk's Vault and connect it to your campaign

steps.name: Install the prerequisites
steps.text: Install Node.js 20 or newer and Git. No Python, no Docker, no database.

steps.name: Get the code onto your machine
steps.text: Clone the repository, or download and extract the ZIP if you would rather not use Git.

steps.name: Launch
steps.text: Run the launcher. It installs dependencies the first time — about a minute — then starts the dashboard on localhost.

steps.name: Configure from the dashboard
steps.text: Choose a model provider, add a key if that provider needs one, and point Vault at the folder holding your campaign documents.

steps.name: Test it
steps.text: Ask a question you know the answer to, and check the citation names the document it came from.

faq.q: Does it make up lore when it does not know?
faq.a: No — that is the whole point of the design. A canonical rule block is appended to every prompt at assembly time, so citation discipline is structural rather than configurable. When the answer is not in your documents the bot emits a fixed refusal phrase, and the question is logged in the dashboard's Lore Gaps tab so you can answer it once and have that answer reused afterwards.

faq.q: Do my campaign documents get uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: Your documents stay in a folder on your machine. Only the question and the snippets that answer it are sent to whichever model you chose, and if you run a local model through Ollama then nothing leaves the machine at all.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: The software is MIT-licensed and free forever. The only cost is the model you pick: Google Gemini's free tier covers most home games, OpenRouter is pay-as-you-go at roughly $0.60 to $4 per three-hour session, a Claude Pro or Max subscription costs nothing extra, and a local model through Ollama costs nothing at all.

faq.q: Do I need to be technical to run it?
faq.a: You need to be comfortable installing Node.js and running a script. On Windows there is a one-file installer that prints its whole plan and asks before it changes anything; on macOS and Linux it is a clone and one command.

faq.q: Can players use it, or only the GM?
faq.a: Both, and how much players can see is yours to set. In Foundry VTT there is a per-world access mode controlling whether players may ask at all, and answers can be whispered rather than posted publicly.

faq.q: What file formats can it read?
faq.a: PDF, DOCX, Markdown, plain text, JSON, YAML, CSV, HTML and RTF. It can also read an existing Obsidian vault directly, strictly read-only, without you having to move or copy anything.

faq.q: Does it work with Foundry VTT?
faq.a: Yes, through a companion module that pairs with your running Vault in one click. You ask with /tusk in the chat bar and the answer posts into the chat log, whispered or public depending on the world's access mode.

faq.q: How is this different from asking ChatGPT about my campaign?
faq.a: A general chatbot will answer every question confidently, including the ones your documents say nothing about, and the invented answer reads exactly like a real one. Vault cites the document behind every claim and refuses when it has no source, which is the behaviour that makes it usable at the table.

faq.q: Does it only work for tabletop campaigns?
faq.a: That is what it was built and tuned for — the prompts, citation styles and refusal wording all assume a game master and a table. But nothing in the machinery knows what a campaign is. It indexes a folder of documents, answers with citations, and refuses when the folder does not cover the question, so pointing it at a handbook, a wiki export, a set of house rules or any other body of documents gives you the same behaviour over those instead.
